summary.summary: Tameside cut borrowing by £20m to £126.269m in 2025/26 — repaying a £10m short-term loan and buying out a £10m Barclays loan early at a c.£2.8m discount — but its cash fell much faster: investments dropped £40.610m to just £22.030m, all in money market funds, as capital spending was funded from balances to defer borrowing in a high-rate market. Interest earned came in £0.886m under budget at £3.789m because balances fell quicker than forecast. £30m of the remaining debt is LOBO loans with semi-annual call options, and Dexia has exercised its option to raise the rate on a £5m LOBO at the 16 June 2026 call date — the council chose to prepay in full and is weighing refinancing. Tameside is also owed £37.440m by Manchester Airport Group (a £29.632m shareholder loan plus £8.954m of COVID-deferred interest); the airport shareholding itself paid no dividend this year, though car-park dividends and loan interest brought in £4.735m.

signals.headline: Dexia exercised the rate-increase option on a £5m LOBO at its 16 June 2026 call date; council electing to prepay in full; £30m of LOBOs remain, all with semi-annual call options (avg 4.42%)
signals.why: Elevated market rates make further calls likely, each forcing repayment from thin cash or refinancing at today's rates.

signals.headline: Treasury investments fell £40.610m in 2025/26 to £22.030m (all money market funds) against £126.269m of borrowing; cash balances fell faster than forecast
signals.why: The internal-borrowing runway is nearly spent, pointing to new short-term borrowing at rates the report says reached 5.0-7.0% late in the year.

signals.headline: £37.440m outstanding from Manchester Airport Group at 31 March 2026 — £29.632m shareholder loan plus £8.954m deferred and accrued interest; the 3.22% MAG shareholding paid no dividend in 2025/26
signals.why: A material single-name exposure whose interest catch-up (£1.146m received this year) depends on the airport group's continued recovery.

signals.headline: Borrowing fell £20m to £126.269m in year, including early repayment of a £10m Barclays loan in December 2025 at a c.£2.8m discount to principal
signals.why: Debt is being actively managed down, and 93.13% of what remains does not mature for at least ten years.

news_drafts.headline: Tameside's schools funding deficit reached £43.873m at 31 March 2026, with about £11m expected from reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Tameside Council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, stood at £43.873m at 31 March 2026. The council's medium-term financial plan for 2027 to 2032, before the Executive Cabinet on 25 November, puts the estimated call on its reserves at around £11m.

The deficit built up through an in-year overspend of £21.783m in 2025/26. The paper says this was driven by overspends in the high needs block, the part of the grant that funds special educational needs, with growth in education, health and care plans behind them. These are the legal plans that set out support for a child with special educational needs.

A statutory override, the temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off a council's main accounts, expires at the end of 2027/28. The council must provide for at least 10% of the deficit at 31 March 2026, plus an estimated 10% of the deficits for 2026/27 and 2027/28.

news_drafts.headline: Tameside forecasts £26.987m schools-grant overspend for 2026/27; balance projected at £154.961m by March 2029
news_drafts.lead:
Tameside Council forecasts an in-year overspend of £26.987m on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) for 2026/27, according to the month 6 budget monitoring update for the Scrutiny Co-ordination and Strategic Improvement Scrutiny Panel. The paper says the overspend is driven by continued growth in demand for Education, Health and Care Plans in the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The paper sets out how the grant's balance is projected to build before any deficit funding. It stood at £43.873m on 31 March 2026 and is projected at £70.863m on 31 March 2027, £109.537m on 31 March 2028 and £154.961m on 31 March 2029. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, is in place to 31 March 2028.

The paper also estimates the council's own share of the balance, after 90% funding of the in-year deficit. That share is put at £4.387m for 2025/26, £2.699m for 2026/27 and £3.867m for 2027/28. The figure for 2028/29 is marked "TBC" in the paper.

news_drafts.headline: Tameside forecasts £70.863m schools grant deficit at March 2027, from £43.873m a year earlier
news_drafts.lead:
Tameside Council forecasts that its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, will carry a cumulative deficit of £70.863m at March 2027, up from £43.873m at 31 March 2026. The figures are in the month 6 budget monitoring, the in-year check of spending against budget, for the Executive Cabinet. The 2025/26 in-year deficit was £21.783m, which the paper attributes to overspends in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), from growth in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs).

The in-year high needs deficit for 2026/27 is forecast at £27.630m, against £29.772m in the original budget and £27.927m forecast in June. Government proposes to fund 90% of deficits accrued to 31 March 2026, subject to Department for Education approval of Tameside's SEND reform plan, submitted in summer 2026. The council expects to hear in early autumn. The council must provide the remaining 10%, plus an estimated 10% of the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits, whose proportions are not yet confirmed. It estimates a call on reserves, money set aside, of around £11m.

The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, is set to expire after 2027/28. The five-year forecast has in-year high needs deficits rising to £51.853m by 2030/31 without significant reforms to funding and net reductions in EHCP numbers. The council expects significant SEND deficit funding in the third quarter of 2026/27, which it says "should support deferral of external borrowing". It has deferred a long-term refinancing decision, taking new loans to repay old ones, on expectations of rates falling. Short-term borrowing stood at £15m at 30 September 2026.

findings.headline: Days lost to sickness absence per FTE rose from 2.60 in Q1 to 3.61 in Q2 2026/27, above the ceiling target of 3.00.
findings.detail: The paper reports 9,879 days lost in the quarter and says sickness rates rose across the organisation. It notes that an Employee Assistance Programme has recently been introduced.
findings.matters: Sickness absence adds cover costs and capacity pressure, which finance directors weigh alongside agency spend and vacancy controls.
findings.figures: 2.60 (days lost per FTE, Q1), 3.61 (Q2), 3.00 (ceiling target), 9,879 (days lost in Q2)
findings.quote: has increased from 2.60 in Q1 to 3.61 in Q2, above the ceiling target of 3.00

findings.headline: 98.8% of EHCPs were issued within the statutory 20-week timescale in Q2 2026/27, up from 66% in Q1.
findings.detail: The paper calls this the third consecutive period of improvement and says Tameside is significantly outperforming the national average of 46.1%. It also reports a DfE stocktake against the 2025 improvement notice.
findings.matters: SEND statutory timeliness is tied to high-needs spending and to inspection outcomes, both of which finance directors watch.
findings.quote: 98.8% of EHCPs were issued within the statutory 20-week timescale, up from 66% in Q1

findings.headline: The number of residents waiting for an Occupational Therapy appointment rose by 111 to 638 in Q2 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to capacity issues within the team. It notes that the Learning Disabilities, Autism and Mental Health teams are reviewing long-term services and that the Adults commissioning strategy is still in progress.
findings.matters: Growing waiting lists for assessment and therapy can translate into later, higher-cost care packages, which finance officers at peer councils track.
findings.quote: rising by an additional 111 people to 638

findings.headline: The 2027/28 budget process began on schedule, with budget challenge sessions held across Quarter 2.
findings.detail: The paper says a communications plan for budget engagement has been agreed, and an update was given to the Scrutiny Co-ordination and Strategic Improvement Scrutiny Panel at the end of the quarter.
findings.matters: The timing and content of a budget process, given the in-year overspend, is one a finance director can compare with their own calendar.
findings.quote: the annual programme began on schedule, with key activities taking place across Quarter 2

findings.headline: The Financial Management service redesign has been implemented, but recruitment to posts other than Assistant Director of Finance has been difficult.
findings.detail: The paper says the redesign included recruitment to the Assistant Director of Finance post. It also records challenges recruiting to other posts in the new structure.
findings.matters: Finance team vacancies affect a council's capacity to deliver budget rebuilds and monitoring, and a finance director at another council may face the same recruitment market.
findings.quote: although the service has faced challenges recruiting to other posts within the structure

daily_post.headline: Capital programme forecast at £68.910m against a revised £69.448m, a £0.538m underspend
daily_post.lead: The reprofiling and underspend affect the timing of borrowing, which the paper says directly drives the revenue cost of treasury management.
